snippet.textDisplay: I have no problem with Georgia being number 1. I do have a problem with a 2-loss Bama team that got blown out, by a team ranked lower than they are, being number 5. That isn't just SEC bias. It's Bama-bias. Just like last year when they got blown out multiple times and still made the playoff over Notre Dame, who was arguably the best team in the nation by year's end (tho they lost two really tight games to good teams to start the season). The CFP better fix this tonight. It's one thing to lose tight games and get quality losses...but when you're consistently getting blown out, I have issues with upvoting teams based on historical merit instead of this season's merit.

snippet.textDisplay:
I'll agree that the SEC is still the premiere conference. However, their record in nonconference games compared to the Big 12 is not something I'd bring up to support that contention. 

Finally, this year saw them add an extra conference game, like the rest of the industrialized world had been doing for decades. But old habits die hard.

You still see the SEC playing the lion's share of their non-con games against schools where the school's head custodian also moonlights as the football team's defensive coordinator. Wofford, The Citadel, and Austin Peay, for example, doubtless fund half their athletic departments' respective budgets through these bodybag games against SEC teams.

snippet.textDisplay: The problem with talking about head-to-head and other things with the AP and coach's poll is that they are compilations of individual people's rankings, unlike the CFP, which I'm pretty sure is just a committee coming to a consensus on one set of rankings as opposed to averaging out all of theirs. Even if a significant number of voters honor a head to head and rank one team just barely above the other, other voters could have the lower team ranked several spots higher for completely different reasons, which entirely throws off the individual pairings.

snippet.textDisplay: The approach of, well this team beat that team a few weeks ago, is flawed and should have little meaning – not none, but little. As I have pointed out before it’s not so much about who has the “best” team, but which team can beat another (and does) on a given day. Especially this year, we have a plethora of examples of one team having beat another even though today we would not say that winner is the better or best team. Let’s face it, in most cases we will not truly know who is a better team without teams playing a series of games, which isn’t going to happen. That’s why consistency may be the single most important factor. Teams need to show they can be ready and perform every time they take the field, not allowing a day such as Georgia did at Auburn and other highly ranked teams have done in other venues.

snippet.textDisplay: Georgia may be better than Utah, but from a resume perspective, they should not be number one.  Yes, the SEC is the best conference by a fairly large margin this year - but still not by so much that offset an undefeated team.   There are advanced math and stats (which really should be used, I mean these teams do supposedly represent institutions of higher learning).   With the limited number of games in college football, it's really hard for schedules to be disproprortionate enough for a team with one or 2 losses to bypass an undefeated team.  Once losses start coming into play though, the schedules start to have an impact.  Texas has such a tough schedule, they should be ahead of Georgia (at this point), even with the extra loss.  But Utah and UCLA should be 1 and 2 (and their resume's are extremely close).   Tennessee and USC should be outside the top 12.  BYU, Houston, Tennessee, and USC are all extremely close, but there is a drop off from Kentucky and TX Tech to them if you're looking at any strength of schedule based on sound math (as opposed to non-transparent ESPN crap).

You are going to take this with a grain of salt because I’m obviously a Bama fan, but I’m saying this as neutral as possible, because I would have no problem with Tennessee being ranked ahead of Bama. 

Based on this poll, Bama is ranked ahead of Tennessee because Bama has wins over #13, #20, and #24. All were on the road and all the wins were by double digits. Tennessee has wins over #7 and #13. Both at home, and a loss to the same #20 team on the road that Bama handled on the road. I think the committee for the CFB and the AP voters are taking the wins on the road into account as well as Bama lost to Tennessee the week after playing Georgia.

It helps Bama that Georgia also lost to Auburn the week after that game. That proves that the Bama vs Georgia game was a huge reason for the results that happened the following week

snippet.textDisplay:
Notre Dame’s 2026 playoff resume is fundamentally less competitive than its top-10 peers week in and week out. This is absolutely due to a lack of sustained  choice of schedule depth ( with competitive teams ), and structural advantage of being able to choose who they want to play always protecting their ability to have a winning record instead of scheduling real competition. While the Week 10 upset over No. 1 Miami is an elite, marquee victory, it stands as an isolated outlier on a schedule that ranks 33rd nationally and completely lacks a week-to-week Power-4 depth by comparison. By fiercely maintaining its independence, Notre Dame bypasses a grueling  nine plus game conference gauntlet, avoiding the physical and mental attrition endured by teams in the SEC, Big Ten or Big Twelve. Furthermore, because the Irish do not belong to a conference, they are completely exempt from playing a high-stakes 13th game in a conference championship. This structural exemption allows Notre Dame to avoid a mandatory postseason elimination game, protects them from an additional loss, and grants them an unearned week of physical rest before the playoffs begin.
Combined, a largely weak schedule, zero conference grind, and the absence of a conference championship game make Notre Dame’s path to the postseason vastly easier and structurally less competitive than the paths of teams fighting through true conference regular seasons. Absolutely trash!

snippet.textDisplay: I disagree. Alabama suffered injuries, but Tennessee did too. Before the season, Tennessee lost its top safety; against Texas, an all-SEC left guard; and during the Georgia Tech game, its best tight end—plus the quarterback was starting his second game. Even with those setbacks, Tennessee controlled every phase of that game. Claiming Alabama’s injuries excuse that performance ignores that everyone is playing injured. Injuries alone do not justify Alabama appearing like frightened children against a team at best equal to them. That is precisely how they looked. At least Georgia showed up in its rivalry with Auburn. Did Alabama ever lead? No, they never held a lead at any point in that game. It was never really close.
